caption:
is hypochlorous acid mist worth it for your face?
It is well proven in wound care. For everyday face use, the evidence is still early.

Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is the key ingredient in the trending face mists. It is also a molecule your own white blood cells make to kill microbes. In wound care it is valued for being antimicrobial while generally well tolerated.

Wound care is where it is most studied. A 2026 review of one pure HOCl wound cleanser pulled together 56 publications and 2,682 patients, including newborns, with no product-related complications reported. Two of its authors work for the manufacturer.

Elsewhere the evidence thins out. It has been studied as an add-on for eyelid inflammation (blepharitis), and in smaller, mixed studies for eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis and acne. A 2025 review across specialties found it useful in most studies, but the results were not entirely consistent and the right dosing is not settled. Daily "calming" and "glow" are not what those studies tested.

Bottles also differ. How much of a product is true hypochlorous acid, rather than hypochlorite, depends on pH and how it was made, and it can drift over time. Storage matters.

What this does not mean: a mist is not an acne treatment. If you like how one feels, that is a fine reason to use it. Just don't expect it to do the job of one.

Amaya R et al. J Wound Care 2026;35(10). doi:10.12968/jowc.2026.0428
Haralovic V et al. Biomedicines 2025. doi:10.3390/biomedicines13122921
Edwards-Jones V. Adv Skin Wound Care 2026. doi:10.1097/ASW.0000000000000524
